<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:F0-main}
Let $n\geq 5$ be odd and let $p_1,\ldots,p_{2n}$ be very general points of $\mathbb F_0=\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1$.
Then
$$
\varepsilon\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbb F_0}(n-4,1);p_1,\ldots,p_{2n}\bigr)=\sqrt{\frac{n-4}{n}}.
$$
The same equality holds when $p_1,\ldots,p_{2n}$ form a very general free orbit of the fixed dihedral group $G_n$ defined in Section~\ref{sec:dihedral}.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:plane-main}
Let $n=2k+1\geq 7$, let
$$
r=k+7=\frac{n+13}{2},
$$
and let $X_r=\operatorname{Bl}_{p_1,\ldots,p_r}\mathbb P^2$ for very general points $p_i$.
Then the divisor
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Ln}
L_n=(3n-4)H-nE_1-(n-2)(E_2+\cdots+E_5)-4(E_6+\cdots+E_{k+5})-2(E_{k+6}+E_{k+7})
\end{equation}
is ample and satisfies
$$
\varepsilon(L_n;x)=2\sqrt{n(n-4)}=\sqrt{L_n^2}
$$
for a very general point $x\in X_r$.
In particular, $\varepsilon(L_n;x)$ is irrational.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:balanced-reflection}
Let $B$ be a smooth connected complex curve with distinguished point $0$, and let $f:\mathcal X\to B$ be a smooth projective threefold whose fibers are smooth projective surfaces.
Assume that the N\'eron--Severi spaces of the fibers are identified by a marking.
Suppose that the special fiber $X_0$ contains a smooth rational curve $\Gamma$ with class $\gamma$ such that
$$
\gamma^2=-2a,\\;\; N_{\Gamma/\mathcal X}\simeq \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-a)\oplus\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-a)
$$
for some integer $a>0$.
If $D\in\operatorname{NS}(X_0)_{\mathbb R}$ is nef, then the marked class
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reflection}
s_\gamma(D)=D+\frac{D\cdot\gamma}{a}\,\gamma
\end{equation}
is nef on very general fibers of $f$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $c$ be an effective integral class on the geometric generic fiber.
After a finite extension of the base field and specialization, $c$ is represented on $X_0$ by an effective divisor $C_0$.
Let $\mu$ be the order of vanishing of the corresponding relative divisor along $\Gamma$.
The first nonzero normal term gives a nonzero homomorphism
$$
\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-c\cdot\gamma)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sym}^{\mu}N_{\Gamma/\mathcal X}^{\vee}\simeq \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(a\mu)^{\oplus(\mu+1)}.
$$
Hence
$$
-c\cdot\gamma\leq a\mu,
$$
while $C_0-\mu\Gamma$ is effective.
Therefore
$$
s_\gamma(c)=c+\frac{c\cdot\gamma}{a}\gamma=(c-\mu\gamma)+\left(\mu+\frac{c\cdot\gamma}{a}\right)\gamma
$$
is represented by an effective real divisor on $X_0$.
The reflection $s_\gamma$ is self-adjoint for the intersection form, so
$$
s_\gamma(D)\cdot c=D\cdot s_\gamma(c)\geq0.
$$
Thus $s_\gamma(D)$ is nef on the geometric generic fiber.
Nefness of a fixed marked class then holds on very general fibers, since the relative Hilbert scheme has only countably many components and the locus where a class of negative intersection becomes effective is a proper closed subset.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:reflection-isometry}
The map $s_\gamma$ is the orthogonal reflection in the hyperplane $\gamma^\perp$.
Indeed, since $\gamma^2=-2a$, formula \eqref{eq:reflection} is the usual expression
$$
s_\gamma(D)=D-2\frac{D\cdot\gamma}{\gamma^2}\gamma.
$$
In particular, it preserves the intersection form and sends isotropic classes to isotropic classes.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:LU-principle}
In the situation of Proposition~\ref{prop:balanced-reflection}, suppose that after identifying a very general fiber with the blow-up $\pi:\widetilde X\to X$ of a smooth projective surface at a point, the reflected class is a positive multiple of
$$
\pi^*L-\sqrt{L^2}\,E
$$
for an ample line bundle $L$ on $X$.
Then
$$
\varepsilon(L;x)=\sqrt{L^2}
$$
for a very general point $x\in X$.
If $L^2$ is not a square, this Seshadri constant is irrational.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{prop:balanced-reflection} gives nefness of the displayed class on a very general fiber, hence $\varepsilon(L;x)\geq\sqrt{L^2}$.
The reverse inequality is the volume bound.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:dJ}
Assume that
$$
c^n\neq1,\\;\; d\notin\{c^w,c^{w-n}\}.
$$
Then there is a birational map $\psi:S\dashrightarrow S$ which lifts to an isomorphism
$$
\widetilde\psi:\operatorname{Bl}_{Z_w(c,d)}S\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Bl}_{Z_w(c,d^*)}S,
\\;\; d^*=\frac{c^{2w-n}}d.
$$
If $H_1,H_2,E_i$ and $H_1',H_2',E_i'$ denote the natural markings on source and target, with corresponding centers labeled by the same first coordinate, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dJ-marking}
\widetilde\psi^*H_1'=H_1,\\;\; \widetilde\psi^*H_2'=nH_1+H_2-E,\\;\; \widetilde\psi^*E_i'=H_1-E_i,
\end{equation}
where $E=\sum_{i=1}^{2n}E_i$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The pullback action of $r_w$ on $H^0(S,\mathcal O_S(n,1))$ has two three-dimensional weight spaces,
$$
\langle1,x^n,x^{n-w}z\rangle,\\;\; \langle x^w,z,x^nz\rangle,
$$
and all remaining weight spaces have dimension two.
Vanishing at $(1,1)$ and $(c,d)$ determines, up to scalar, the sections
\begin{align*}
\sigma_0&=c^n-dc^{n-w}+(dc^{n-w}-1)x^n+(1-c^n)x^{n-w}z,\\
\sigma_1&=d(c^n-1)x^w+(c^w-dc^n)z+(d-c^w)x^nz.
\end{align*}
After bihomogenization, write $\sigma_i=A_i z_0+B_i z_1$.
A direct determinant calculation gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:determinant}
A_0B_1-A_1B_0=-(c^w-d)(c^{n-w}d-1)(x_1^n-x_0^n)(x_1^n-c^nx_0^n).
\end{equation}
Under our assumptions the right-hand side has precisely $2n$ simple zeros in the first factor, and the coefficient matrix has rank one at each zero.
Since $(nH_1+H_2)^2=2n$, the base scheme of the pencil $\langle\sigma_0,\sigma_1\rangle$ is the reduced set $Z_w(c,d)$.
Thus
$$
\psi(x,z)=\left(x,\frac{\sigma_1(x,z)}{d\sigma_0(x,z)}\right)
$$
is resolved by blowing up these $2n$ points and contracts the strict transforms of the $2n$ first-ruling fibers through them.
The target is again $S$, blown up at the images of the contracted fibers.
Evaluating on $x=1$ and $x=c$ gives second coordinates $1$ and $c^{2w-n}/d$, respectively, hence the target centers form $Z_w(c,d^*)$.
The formulas \eqref{eq:dJ-marking} follow from the pencil and from the classes of the contracted curves.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:nondegenerate}
For every $j\geq0$ the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:dJ} are satisfied by $(c_j,d_j,w_j)$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Starting from $(\rho_0,\tau_0)=(n-2,1)$, induction using \eqref{eq:exponent-recurrence} shows that
$$
|\rho_j|>|\tau_j|>0
$$
for all $j$.
At even steps the two exponents have the same sign, and at odd steps they have opposite signs.
Indeed, the first transformation sends a same-sign pair with $|\rho|>|\tau|$ to an opposite-sign pair with the same strict inequality, while the second transformation sends an opposite-sign pair to a same-sign pair because $n-4\geq1$, and for $n\geq5$ the first component has strictly larger absolute value than the second.
Thus $c_j^n\neq1$.
Moreover the forbidden equalities $\tau_j=w_j\rho_j$ and $\tau_j=(w_j-n)\rho_j$ are impossible because $|\tau_j/\rho_j|<1$, whereas
$$
|w_j|>1,\\;\; |w_j-n|>1
$$
for $w_j\in\{(n-1)/2,n-2\}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:R-nef}
The class $R_n$ is nef on $X_0=\operatorname{Bl}_{G_n\cdot(1,1)}S$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The characteristic polynomial of $T_n$ is
$$
(t-1)\bigl(t^2-(n-2)t+1\bigr).
$$
Its dominant eigenvalue is
$$
\lambda=\frac{n-2+\Delta}{2}>1.
$$
Set
$$
\overline R_n=\beta H_1+\alpha H_2-E,\\;\; K=-2H_1-2H_2+E.
$$
A direct calculation gives
$$
T_n(R_n)=\lambda R_n,\\;\; T_n(\overline R_n)=\lambda^{-1}\overline R_n,\\;\; T_n(K)=K.
$$
Moreover
\begin{equation}\label{eq:H2-decomposition}
H_2=\frac{\beta}{n(n-4)}R_n+\frac{\alpha}{n(n-4)}\overline R_n+\frac1{n-4}K.
\end{equation}
For every $j$, the class $T_n^j(H_2)$ is the pullback of a ruling class under a composition of the isomorphisms $f_i$, hence is nef.
Multiplying \eqref{eq:H2-decomposition} by $\lambda^{-j}$ after applying $T_n^j$ shows that a positive multiple of $R_n$ is the limit of nef classes.
Since the nef cone is closed, $R_n$ is nef.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:reflected-ray}
The reflected class $s_\gamma(R_n)$ is a positive multiple of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Seshadri-ray}
(n-4)H_1+H_2-\sqrt{\frac{n-4}{n}}\,E.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Substitute \eqref{eq:Rn} and \eqref{eq:gamma} into the reflection formula.
Using $\Delta^2=n(n-4)$ gives
$$
s_\gamma(R_n)=c_n\left((n-4)H_1+H_2-\frac{\Delta}{n}E\right),
$$
where
$$
c_n=\frac{n(n-3)+(n-1)\Delta}{4}>0.
$$
Since $\Delta/n=\sqrt{(n-4)/n}$, this is \eqref{eq:Seshadri-ray} up to the positive scalar $c_n$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:normal-bundle}
One has
$$
N_{\Gamma_0/\mathcal X}\simeq \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-2)\oplus\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-2).
$$
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Before blowing up the moving sections, the normal bundle of $\Gamma\simeq\mathbb P^1$ in $S\times B$ is
$$
\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(2n-4)\oplus\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1},
$$
because $\Gamma^2=2(n-2)$ in $S$ and the parameter direction contributes the trivial summand.
Each of the $2n$ blow-ups performs an elementary transform and lowers the total degree by one.
Hence, for the resulting rank-two bundle $N=N_{\Gamma_0/\mathcal X}$,
$$
\deg N=(2n-4)-2n=-4.
$$
It remains to prove $H^0(N(1))=0$.

Use the affine normal coordinate
$$
v=z-x^{n-2}
$$
near $\Gamma$.
For the first $n$ moving sections one has $x^n=1$ at $t=0$ and the normal slope is
$$
v'=-(n-2)x^{n-2},
$$
while for the other $n$ sections one has $x^n=u^n$ and
$$
v'=(n-2)x^{n-2}.
$$
A section of $N(1)$ is represented on the affine chart by a pair of polynomials $(f,g)$ with
$$
\deg f\leq2n-3,\\;\; \deg g\leq1,
$$
satisfying the elementary-transform conditions at the $2n$ orbit points.
Equivalently, there exist polynomials $a,b$ of degree at most $n-3$ such that
\begin{align}
 f+(n-2)x^{n-2}g&=(x^n-1)a,\label{eq:normal1}\\
 f-(n-2)x^{n-2}g&=(x^n-u^n)b.\label{eq:normal2}
\end{align}
Subtracting \eqref{eq:normal2} from \eqref{eq:normal1}, the coefficients in degrees $n,\ldots,2n-3$ force $a=b$.
We then obtain
$$
2(n-2)x^{n-2}g=(u^n-1)a.
$$
The left-hand side is supported only in degrees $n-2$ and $n-1$, whereas the right-hand side has degree at most $n-3$.
Thus $g=a=b=0$, and then $f=0$.
Hence $H^0(N(1))=0$.

By Grothendieck splitting, write $N\simeq\mathcal O(r)\oplus\mathcal O(s)$.
The vanishing of $H^0(N(1))$ gives $r,s\leq-2$, while $r+s=-4$.
Therefore $r=s=-2$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
On the special fiber, Proposition~\ref{prop:R-nef} gives the nef isotropic class $R_n$.
The curve $\Gamma_0$ has class $\gamma$ with $\gamma^2=-4$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:normal-bundle} gives
$$
N_{\Gamma_0/\mathcal X}\simeq\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-2)^{\oplus2}.
$$
Proposition~\ref{prop:balanced-reflection} therefore shows that $s_\gamma(R_n)$ is nef on very general fibers of the one-parameter family.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:reflected-ray}, a positive multiple of
$$
(n-4)H_1+H_2-\sqrt{\frac{n-4}{n}}\,E
$$
is nef on such fibers.

The same marked class is then nef on a very general free $G_n$-orbit.
Indeed, in the irreducible parameter space of free orbits, every integral class having negative intersection with the marked class has an effectivity locus which is closed and does not contain the orbit already obtained above.
There are only countably many integral classes.
The identical argument in the irreducible parameter space of ordered $2n$-tuples of distinct points shows nefness for $2n$ very general points of $S$.

Since
$$
\mathcal O_S(n-4,1)^2=2(n-4),
$$
the volume bound is
$$
\sqrt{\frac{2(n-4)}{2n}}=\sqrt{\frac{n-4}{n}}.
$$
The constructed nef class gives the reverse inequality, so equality holds.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:irrational-multipoint}
For $n>4$ the number $\sqrt{(n-4)/n}$ is irrational.
Indeed, if $n(n-4)=m^2$, then
$$
(n-2-m)(n-2+m)=4.
$$
For odd $n$ both factors are positive even integers, forcing both to equal $2$, which is impossible for $n>4$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:quotient-epsilon}
For a very general smooth point $y\in Y$ one has
$$
\varepsilon(A;y)=2\sqrt{n(n-4)}.
$$
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Choose $p\in S$ with trivial stabilizer and put $y=q(p)$.
The blow-up of $S$ along the free orbit $G_n\cdot p$ maps finitely to $\operatorname{Bl}_yY$, and the exceptional divisor over $y$ pulls back to the sum of the $2n$ exceptional curves upstairs.
Nefness can be tested after finite pullback.
Using \eqref{eq:A-pullback} and Theorem~\ref{thm:F0-main}, we obtain
$$
\varepsilon(A;y)=2n\sqrt{\frac{n-4}{n}}=2\sqrt{n(n-4)}.
$$
The assertion holds at a very general smooth point because the quotient of the very general free-orbit locus is very general in $Y$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:Cminusone}
The curve $C$ is a section of $f$ with
$$
C^2=-1.
$$
It meets $U_1$ and $U_2$ in the two finite reducible fibers and meets $G_1$ in the fiber over infinity.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The curve $B$ has class $2H_1+H_2$ and hence $B^2=4$.
Since $B\to B/G_n$ has degree $2n$, the image $\overline B\subset Y$ satisfies
$$
\overline B^2=\frac{4}{2n}=\frac2n.
$$
The curve $\overline B$ passes through one $A_1$ point in each finite reducible fiber, contributing a correction $1/2$ at each point to the self-intersection of its strict transform.
It also passes through the cyclic quotient point of type $\frac1n(1,2)$.
In the resolution chain $[-(k+1),-2]$, the curve $C$ meets the component $G_1$ transversely.
The corresponding diagonal entry of the inverse of the positive intersection matrix
$$
\begin{pmatrix}k+1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}
$$
is $2/n$.
Therefore
$$
C^2=\frac2n-\frac12-\frac12-\frac2n=-1.
$$
The assertions about the components met by $C$ follow from the local equations of $B$ and from the construction of the quotient fibers.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:M-plane}
In the plane marking above,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:M-plane}
M=(3n-2)h-(n-2)e_1-n(e_2+e_3+e_4+e_5)-4(e_6+\cdots+e_{k+5})-2(e_{k+6}+e_{k+7}).
\end{equation}
In particular,
$$
M^2=4n(n-4)=A^2.
$$
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Write
$$
M=dh-\sum_{i=1}^{k+7}m_ie_i.
$$
Since $C=e_1$ and $F=h-e_1$, equations \eqref{eq:MC-MF} give
$$
m_1=n-2,\\;\; d-m_1=2n,
$$
so $d=3n-2$.
Orthogonality to $W_1,W_2$ gives
$$
m_2=m_3,\\;\; m_4=m_5,
$$
and orthogonality to $U_1,U_2$ then gives
$$
m_2=m_3=m_4=m_5=n.
$$

At infinity, orthogonality to $G_2$ gives $m_{k+6}=m_{k+7}$, orthogonality to $H_1$ gives $m_{k+5}=2m_{k+6}$, and the remaining $H_j$ show that
$$
m_6=\cdots=m_{k+5}=2m_{k+6}.
$$
Finally, $M\cdot G_1=0$ yields
$$
\sum_{i=6}^{k+6}m_i=2n.
$$
Since $n=2k+1$, this becomes
$$
(2k+1)m_{k+6}=2n,
$$
so $m_{k+6}=m_{k+7}=2$ and $m_6=\cdots=m_{k+5}=4$.
This proves \eqref{eq:M-plane}.
The self-intersection is either computed directly or follows from $M=\nu^*A$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:Hanumanthu}
Let $X\to\mathbb P^2$ be the blow-up at $r$ general points and let
$$
L=dH-\sum_{i=1}^r m_iE_i,
$$
where $m_1\geq\cdots\geq m_r>0$.
Then $L$ is ample if the following inequalities hold:
\begin{align*}
d&>m_1+m_2,\\
2d&>m_1+\cdots+m_5,\\
3d&>2m_1+m_2+\cdots+m_7,
\end{align*}
and, for every $2\leq s\leq r$,
$$
d^2\geq\frac{s+3}{s+2}\sum_{i=1}^s m_i^2.
$$
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:ample}
For every odd $n=2k+1\geq7$, the divisor $L_n$ from \eqref{eq:Ln} is ample on the blow-up of $k+7$ general points of $\mathbb P^2$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Order the multiplicities as
$$
n,\quad (n-2)^4,\quad 4^k,\quad 2^2.
$$
Set $d=3n-4$.
The first three inequalities in Theorem~\ref{thm:Hanumanthu} become
\begin{align*}
3n-4&>2n-2,\\
6n-8&>5n-8,\\
9n-12&>6n,
\end{align*}
and all hold for $n\geq7$.

For the last family of inequalities, observe that for every $s\geq2$,
$$
\frac{s+3}{s+2}\leq\frac54.
$$
Moreover the sum of the squares of all multiplicities is
$$
\Sigma=n^2+4(n-2)^2+16k+8=5n^2-8n+16.
$$
Hence it is enough to prove
$$
d^2>\frac54\Sigma.
$$
After clearing denominators this is
$$
4(3n-4)^2-5(5n^2-8n+16)=11n^2-56n-16>0.
$$
The last expression is positive at $n=7$ and is strictly increasing for $n\geq7$.
Thus all hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:Hanumanthu} are satisfied.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{prop:ample} proves that $L_n$ is ample.
The nef class \eqref{eq:nef-Ln} gives
$$
\varepsilon(L_n;x)\geq2\sqrt{n(n-4)}
$$
at a very general point.
By \eqref{eq:Lsquare}, the volume bound gives the reverse inequality.
Therefore
$$
\varepsilon(L_n;x)=2\sqrt{n(n-4)}.
$$
Finally, $n(n-4)$ is not a square for $n>4$ by Remark~\ref{rem:irrational-multipoint}, so the Seshadri constant is irrational.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:natural-divisor}
Before the quadratic transformation one obtains the equally explicit divisor
$$
M_n^{\mathrm{pl}}=(3n-2)H-n(E_1+E_2+E_3+E_4)-(n-2)E_5-4(E_6+\cdots+E_{k+5})-2(E_{k+6}+E_{k+7}),
$$
after reordering the coefficients of \eqref{eq:M-plane}.
It also has square $4n(n-4)$ and the same maximal Seshadri constant at a very general point.
The quadratic transformation is used only to obtain the more reduced expression \eqref{eq:Ln}.
For $n=5$, two quadratic transformations starting from the natural plane-model class recover the divisor $9H-3(E_1+\cdots+E_5)-2(E_6+\cdots+E_9)$ of Laface--Ugaglia.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
Can the balanced-reflection principle be combined with a dynamical nef ray on a smooth family in such a way that the quotient step is avoided altogether?
In particular, can one obtain infinite families of irrational one-point Seshadri constants on smooth surfaces of fixed Picard number?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
For even values of $n$, can one replace the present choice of weights by a different dihedral or more general finite-group action so that the de Jonqui\`eres iteration remains nondegenerate and produces an analogous irrational limiting ray?
<!-- end question-2 -->
